data.copy:
Psalm 23 is the most memorized passage in the entire Bible.

It is read at every funeral. Whispered at every bedside. Recited by men who have never opened a Bible in their lives.

And almost nobody knows what any of it actually means.

"The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want."

Every Christian can finish the rest from memory. The green pastures.

The still waters. The valley of the shadow of death. The rod and the staff. The table. The overflowing cup.

Beautiful poetry. Familiar words. Profound comfort.

And every single line is describing something specific, physical, and real that most men have never been told.

Because we do not know what a shepherd actually did.

David did. He was one. And he was not writing poetry. He was writing a job description.

Here is what Psalm 23 says when you understand what an ancient Middle Eastern shepherd did for his sheep.

"He makes me lie down in green pastures."

Sheep do not lie down on their own. They are prey animals wired for constant fear. A sheep will not rest unless it is free from danger, free from friction with the other sheep, free from parasites, and free from hunger.

A shepherd who makes his sheep lie down has solved every source of fear in their lives. They are not resting because they chose to. They are resting because he made it safe enough to stop running.

"He leads me beside still waters."

Sheep are terrified of moving water. Their wool soaks it up and they drown. A shepherd never leads his flock to a rushing stream. He finds a calm pool, or dams a stream with rocks to make the water still.

He reshapes the world around them so they can drink without dying.

"He restores my soul."

The Hebrew behind "restores" carries the idea of turning back, bringing back. It is the picture of a shepherd who goes out, finds the sheep that wandered off a cliff or into a thicket, and carries it home on his shoulders.

It is not a metaphor. It is a rescue.

"Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death."

data.copy:
There are five types of people who are certain they are saved but according to Jesus, many of them are not. 

I am going to walk through all five. Read each one closely. 

Type one. The cultural Christian. 

He grew up in it. Christian parents. Church every Sunday. Maybe a Christian school. He owns three Bibles and knows the songs by heart. 

And somewhere along the way he assumed that being surrounded by it made him part of it. 

But Jesus told Nicodemus, a man who knew Scripture backwards and forwards, that you must be born again. He said humans reproduce only human life. Your parents can hand you their name, their values, their upbringing, their inheritance. They cannot hand you their salvation. 

You can sit at a five star chef's table every night of your life and still not know how to cook a single thing. Proximity is not possession. 

About six in ten Americans call themselves Christian. When one study asked the deeper question, whether their hope of heaven rested on personally trusting Christ, roughly one in three said yes. 

Type two. The aisle walker. 

He did come to God once. There was a night at camp, or a Sunday when the music was right, and he walked down front and prayed the prayer. Maybe he got baptized. He felt something real. 

Jesus described this in the parable of the soils. The seed on rocky ground represents people who hear the message and immediately receive it with joy. Notice, immediately and with joy. This is not a cold or hostile man. He responded. 

But there was no root. And when trouble came, he fell away. 

Nobody is saying your moment was not genuine. What I am saying is that a card you signed twenty years ago is not the same as a life. The question is what happened after. If there is no Bible, no prayer, no fruit, no change, nothing at all in the years since, that is worth sitting with honestly.

data.caption: dearpersonco.store
data.copy:
There was a night I sat in my truck in the driveway and did the math on whether my kids would be better off without me.

I'm 100 pounds lighter now.

That's not the part of this story that matters.

Every insecure bone in my body is telling me not to post this. I've started and stopped about ten times.

But I think there's a dad out there right now doing the same math I did, and if there's even a chance he reads this before he finishes it, then me being embarrassed doesn't count for much.

So I'm going to tell you the truth.

I need to explain that math to you, because if you've never been there, it sounds insane.

And if you have been there, you already know it doesn't feel insane at all.

It feels like the most responsible thing you've ever calculated.

Here's how the lie works on a father.

It doesn't come at you screaming. It comes at you reasonable. Calm. Almost gentle.

It says: look at you. Look what you let yourself become.

It says: there's a life insurance policy. The mortgage would be covered. They'd be taken care of.

It says: they deserve a dad who plays outside, not one who falls asleep in the recliner at 7 every night.

It says: you're not really a father anymore. You're a weight the whole family is carrying.

And then it does the cruelest thing of all.

It tells you that leaving would be the last good thing you could still do for them.

It dresses the worst idea you've ever had up in the clothing of love.

That's why it almost works. Because it doesn't feel like giving up.

It feels like a gift you'd be giving them.

I let myself go for years before that night. The body was just the receipt for everything happening on the inside.

I ate to feel something. Then I ate to feel nothing. Then I just ate because stopping meant sitting alone with my own head, and that was the one place I refused to go.

I stopped looking in mirrors. My wedding ring stopped fitting and I told my wife I'd get it resized and I never did. It's still in a drawer somewhere.

I wa…

data.caption: Read This If Hip Pain Is Stealing Your Life ☝️
data.copy:
My bone-on-bone hip pain has cost me over three thousand pounds in five years on Voltarol, Holland and Barrett supplements, magnetic patches from the Daily Mail and a copper bracelet that never moved the pain. Then I read what an NHS surgeon wrote.

My name is Margaret. I'm 64, I live in a small terraced house in a quiet town in Nottinghamshire, and I retired three years ago after thirty years working as a senior care assistant in a residential home. My husband Tony is 66, a retired electrician. We have two grown children and three grandchildren, the youngest only eighteen months old.

The hip pain started in 2020. A dull ache in the right groin walking up the garden path. The X-ray two years later confirmed bone-on-bone osteoarthritis, right hip, advanced. The GP gave me the same prescription she'd been giving everybody. Lose half a stone, take paracetamol, try ibuprofen if it gets worse.

That was the start of five years of money spent on things that never moved the pain.

This morning I opened the bathroom cabinet to get the toothpaste. I stood there for a minute counting what was in front of me.

Voltarol gel from Boots. Nineteen pounds fifty a tube. I'd been using it for over two years before I learned it only penetrates the first five millimetres of skin. The actual hip joint is two inches below that. The gel was sitting on skin that wasn't even where the pain was.

Turmeric capsules from Holland and Barrett. Eighteen pounds a bottle. Three different brands over the years. The most recent one was still sealed because I knew it wouldn't work this time either.

Magnesium tablets. Twelve pounds. I'd taken them every day for over a year. My GP confirmed my blood magnesium was within normal range. Not a noticeable difference in the deep groin pain.

data.caption: Read This If You Have Gum Recession ☝️
data.copy:
I remember sitting in the periodontist's waiting room, holding that $5,800 estimate, thinking… there has to be another way.

The paper they handed me had line items. Palatal graft. Anesthesia. Post-op care. Like a receipt for something I never agreed to buy.

I folded it and put it in my purse. Couldn't look at it anymore.

That was eight months ago. I'm 52. I've had the same dentist for 14 years. I thought I was doing everything right.

I'm not the kind of person who skips checkups. I have a Sonicare I paid too much for. I floss. Not every night, but most nights. I use the prescription fluoride toothpaste they gave me two years ago when my pockets started getting deeper.

But at my appointment in October, my hygienist called out numbers I hadn't heard before. 5. 6. Bleeding. 6. Another 5.

My dentist came in after. Sat down. Which they only do when the news is bad.

"Your recession has progressed significantly since your last visit. We're at the point where we need to refer you to a periodontist."

I asked what that meant exactly.

She said gum graft surgery. Tissue taken from the roof of my mouth. Stitched over the exposed roots. Recovery takes weeks. Insurance covers almost none of it.

I drove home and cried in the parking garage for about ten minutes before I pulled myself together.

I'm not a dramatic person. But something about sitting in that chair, under those lights, being told that the only fix for my deteriorating mouth involved someone slicing open my palate… it broke something in me a little.

The shame was the worst part. I kept thinking, how did I let it get this bad. I brush. I've been going to the dentist twice a year since I was a kid. My mother had dentures by 60 and I swore that would never be me.

And here I was.

I told my sister that night and she said "well just get the surgery." Like it was nothing. Like five thousand dollars and weeks of recovery and someone cutting the roof of my mouth open was just… a Tuesday.

data.caption: Back in lane four
data.copy:
My best friend and I have shared everything for forty-one years.

The same street.

The same church pew.

The same dress size, give or take a Christmas.

Last March, I decided we shared a liver disease.

I was wrong, and being wrong is the only reason you're reading this letter.

My name is Diane.

I am 59 years old, I live in eastern Wisconsin, and until two years ago I was the school secretary who ran the front office of the same elementary school for thirty-one years, which means there is nothing your child can do that surprises me and no excuse I haven't heard twice.

Patty lives four houses down.

We raised our kids across each other's kitchens.

We sing next to each other in the choir.

And for twenty-two years, we swam.

Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday, six in the morning, lane four at the Y, with the same three women, through two knee surgeries that weren't ours and one pastor scandal that also wasn't ours, thank you.

My swim bag lived by the front door for two decades.

Gary used to say the house smelled faintly of chlorine and he'd stopped noticing, the way you stop noticing anything that's just true.

I'm telling you about the swimming because of how quietly it ended.

Not with a decision.

With excuses.

A cold that turned into a busy stretch.

A busy stretch that turned into winter.

Patty's hip, my whatever.

The bag migrated from the front door to the hall closet, and then to the back of the hall closet, and the Y kept charging us both every month, and neither of us canceled, because canceling would have made it true.

And while the swimming was quietly ending, other quiet things were starting.

I moved my bra to the last hook and told myself the dryer did it.

The crease from my pillow started staying on my face past nine in the morning.

Then past ten.

There's a church directory photo from that spring where I look like I'm holding my breath, and I wasn't, that's just where my face lived by then.

data.caption: Back in lane four
data.copy:
Patty and I have been best friends for forty-one years, and last March she called me on a Tuesday afternoon and said three words that rearranged my year.

I have fatty liver.

Non-alcoholic, she kept saying, like the word alcoholic was the part that stung.

By one in the morning I had decided I had it too.

We have the same body, Patty and I.

Same soft middle, same full morning face, same ankles by supper, forty-one years of matching everything, and now her everything had a diagnosis, so I gave it to mine.

Three weeks later, a doctor who has known me sixteen years told me my liver was completely fine.

And then I asked him the question this whole letter exists to answer.

Then why do I look exactly like her?

What he said sent me to a system in my own body nobody had ever named to me, and it ends, for now, in lane four of the YMCA pool at six in the morning, where this story should have been living all along.

But it starts with the swimming, and how quietly it ended.

My name is Diane.

I am 59 years old, I live in eastern Wisconsin, and until two years ago I was the school secretary who ran the front office of the same elementary school for thirty-one years, which means there is nothing your child can do that surprises me and no excuse I haven't heard twice.

Patty lives four houses down.

We raised our kids across each other's kitchens.

We sing next to each other in the choir.

And for twenty-two years, we swam.

Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday, six in the morning, lane four at the Y, with the same three women, through two knee surgeries that weren't ours and one pastor scandal that also wasn't ours, thank you.

My swim bag lived by the front door for two decades.

Gary used to say the house smelled faintly of chlorine and he'd stopped noticing, the way you stop noticing anything that's just true.

data.caption: metabolae.com
data.copy:
I am in a hospital bed. If you are a type 2 diabetic and your doctor keeps telling you to just take m*tformin and manage your A1c, I am begging you to listen to me right now.

I had a heart attack two weeks ago.

I almost did not make it, and I am writing this because if I had seen something like it a year ago, I would not be here.

I placed my 1,412th coronary stent on October 3rd, 2024.

Sixteen days later, at 2:47 AM on October 19th, I was on the receiving end of one.

I was 58 years old.

I am a board-certified interventional cardiologist. Twenty-two years of practice. Two stents placed in my own left anterior descending artery by a fellow I had trained three years earlier.

I coded on the table for eleven seconds.

The hospital bill was $71,000. Cardiac rehab was another $9,200.

They will let me operate again. My hospital privileges are intact. But I will never place a stent again without remembering that I was on that same table with someone I had trained running a wire into my own artery because everything I was taught to prescribe had not saved me.

I am writing this because I know exactly what my colleagues will say when they see it. I do not care.

If you are over 50 and you have Type 2 diabetes, or someone you love does, please read the entire thing.

I know it is long. I know you are scrolling. I know you have things to do.

Fifteen months ago I would have given anything for someone with my credential to sit me down and tell me what I am about to tell you.

Nobody did.

I was diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes six years ago at 52. Fasting glucose 141. A1C 6.9.

The diagnosis surprised me and it did not. My father had died of a myocardial infarction at 64. He was a Type 2 diabetic managed on M*tformin and a blood pressure pill for eleven years. My mother's blood pressure had been creeping upward for a decade before she passed. I had watched the pattern in my own family and I had built my entire practice on treating cardiac events in patients who looked like …

data.caption: junkjournalguide.com
data.copy:
There is probably a drawer somewhere in your home filled with things you could never bring yourself to throw away.

Birthday cards with familiar handwriting.

Old photographs that never made it into an album.

A receipt from a memorable trip.

A ribbon from a meaningful gift.

A recipe card covered in little stains from years of use.

To anyone else, they may look like ordinary scraps.

But you know why you saved them.

The problem is that these memories often remain hidden for years. We move them from one drawer to another, promising ourselves that someday we will organise them properly.

Junk journaling offers a different way.

You can turn an envelope into a pocket, place a photograph inside it, add a strip of lace and write a few words about why that moment mattered.

You do not have to document your entire life at once.

Begin with one memory.

One photograph.

One small piece you were never ready to throw away.

The Junk Journaling Guide shows beginners how to organise these keepsakes into pages, pockets, tags and layered journal spreads that feel meaningful—not cluttered.

You do not need perfect handwriting or expensive supplies. The worn edges, faded colours and little imperfections are what make the finished journal personal.

Do not let the pieces of your story remain forgotten inside a drawer.

The printable guide is free today. Just cover the small processing fee while the offer is available.
data.description: Turn photographs, notes and scraps into personal journal pages.

keyword.description: Free-text search string (lowercased server-side). Use for product names, brands, hooks, domains — not for category/niche (use niches).
keyword.allowed_values: Any string; empty = no text filter.

searchkeyword.description: Which ad field keyword searches. NOT a niche/category selector.
searchkeyword.allowed_values: All, landingurl, pagename, adtext, productname. Default All when keyword is set.

countries.description: Ad target countries (where the ad runs — wlads.countries). Not store HQ.
countries.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.
countries.notes: MX/CO/CL are not in this Meta targeting catalog. Use store_based_in for stores based in those markets.

excludeCountries.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.

storebasedin.description: Store Based In (dashboard storebasedin → store_traffic.shop_origin_country). Use for Mexico/Colombia/Chile/etc. store HQ.
storebasedin.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2 including MX, CO, CL, AR, PE and other Explore Shops Based In markets.

niches.description: Product category / vertical filter (dashboard Meta niches). Use when user asks for a category, niche, vertical, or market — not keyword.
niches.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: CG, AM, GG, JY, GS, HT, BY, BG, SK, WC, MC, SP, KS, TS, HE, PS, DP, HI, FT, OG, OP, TR, AC, AA, BM, FK, SH, SW, EL, FW, WT, EW, FR, GM, PH, EC, WE, SC, BE, MU, PA, CB, CF, CP, DC, CT, HH, SG, YG, CC, PZ, LS, GP, WN, SF, OR, MG, PB. See allowed_niches in response for code→label map. Fashion/clothing = CG.

website.description: Detected store/checkout technology on the landing page (dashboard Website filter).
website.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: SH, TP, BU, LS, CC, SL, TA, GG, FU, CS, LP, FO, SI, GP, XS, YC, HY, DI, MS, SB, PP, WC, TT, TW, PI, GO, SC, FB, MG, WP, SQ, PS, GM, KV, CO, HJ, WX, AR, BC, MC. SH=Shopify, WC=WooCommerce, CS=Clickfunnels. See allowed_technologies in response.

languages.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

excludeLanguages.allowed_values: Comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

apps.description: Shopify apps detected on the store.
apps.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated app names/ids from dashboard Apps filter. See allowed_apps in response.

excludeApps.description: Exclude stores using these Shopify apps.
excludeApps.allowed_values: Comma-separated app names/ids. See allowed_apps in response.

themes.description: Shopify theme name on the store (exact match).
themes.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated exact theme names from dashboard Themes filter (discover via GET /api/themes).

scaling.allowed_values: rising, stable, declining, nodownscaling, upscaling, downscaling.

mediafilter.allowed_values: videos, images, carousel, dco. Omit/All = all formats.

pagetypefilter.allowed_values: products, collections, funnels, nofunnels. Empty/All = all types.

adscorefilter.description: WinningHunter ad score tier (Established / Has Potential / Unestablished).
adscorefilter.allowed_values: winning (Established), scaling (Has Potential), testing (Unestablished). Requires matching account tier.

lowimpressions.description: Hide ads with very low impressions.
lowimpressions.allowed_values: hide (exclude low-impression rows). Omit = show all.

rankgrowthfilter.description: Within-brand ad rank momentum vs historic rank_history.
rankgrowthfilter.allowed_values: Comma-separated subset of: rising, stable, declining.

minadrank.description: Minimum within-brand ad rank (lower rank number = stronger ad for that brand, e.g. #1).

min.description: Minimum duplicate/active-seen ad count on the page.

minactiveads.description: Minimum active Meta ads on the advertiser Facebook page (total_active_ads_on_page).
minactiveads.notes: find_winning_products auto-applies minactiveads=50 for US when not set (see forced block).

minactiveadsgrowth.description: Minimum page active-ads percent growth over activeadsgrowthperiod.
minactiveadsgrowth.allowed_values: Human percent (25 = 25%); negatives allowed for decline.

activeadsgrowthperiod.description: Lookback window for active-ads growth filter.
activeadsgrowthperiod.allowed_values: 1w, 1m, 3m. Default 1m when min/max growth set. 1w=1 week, 1m=1 month, 3m=3 months.
activeadsgrowthperiod.notes: 14d/2m exist on the dashboard but are omitted from MCP — sparse wlads baselines return empty result sets.

minpagelikes.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. Ads missing the field excluded when min set.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.

allowed_apps: BOGOS.io Free Gift Buy X Get Y
KB Back In Stock Restock Alert
Sticky Add To Cart Booster Pro
POWR Email Popup Sales Pop Ups
EG Auto Add to Cart Free Gift
SA Request a Quote, Hide Price
Zoorix Sticky Add To Cart Bar
Tada Pop up Spin Wheel Popups
Coupon X: Discount Code Pop Up
SC Back in Stock Restock Alert

mcp_pagination.hint: Pass scroll_next as scroll on the next call with the same filters to continue. Do not rely on page alone.
